title: UMAI: UM Aware Inference with a Frozen Qwen3-ASR
summary: Speech recognizers often leave filled pauses such as uh and um out of the transcript. Fine-tuning on verbatim transcripts can bring them back, but it can also change the rest of the output. We show that most missing fillers can be recovered from values recorded during a single greedy decoding pass of a frozen recognizer, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B. For each gap between output words, UMAI (UM Aware Inference) pools frame-class posteriors over an audio window located by decoder attention. It combines them with the decoder states through two stages of linear discriminant analysis and calibrates the score by isotonic regression. No parameter is trained by gradient descent. UMAI inserts [uh] and [um] tags and leaves every recognized word unchanged. On the held-out AMI evaluation set, filler F1 rises from 12.2 to 82.6. On the Nyra verbatim benchmark, where the operating threshold was chosen, it rises from 37.2 to 96.5. Total processing time increases by 14%.

title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
comment: Accepted at the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 2026
summary: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.

title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
comment: Accepted at the 23rd Sound and Music Computing Conference (SMC), 2026
summary: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.

title: Investigation of generalization to unseen audio generation models in audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction
summary: Text-to-audio generation (TTA) requires reliable evaluation of semantic alignment between generated audio and input text. Existing learning-based alignment-score prediction models have been evaluated only on audio generated by models included in the training data, leaving their generalization to unseen generation models unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the generalization of audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction models to unseen TTA models and introduce adversarial training using a generation-model classifier with a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Experimental results show that pretrained audio encoders capture generation-model-specific characteristics and that alignment-score prediction performance degrades on audio generated by unseen TTA models. Applying the GRL improves prediction performance in some settings, although its effectiveness in suppressing generation-model-specific information is limited.

title: Line-Level Singer Diarization in Multi-Member Pop Songs: A Benchmark, Lead-Vocal Isolation, and Song-Level Decoding
summary: Fans of multi-member pop groups annotate songs line by line with the member who sings each line, but speech diarization does not transfer to this setting: a commercial diarizer finds one or two speakers in songs by groups of four to eight. We study line-level singer diarization: given a song and its lyric-line timings, group the lines by singer with no prior knowledge of the group. We release ColorCoded-SD, a benchmark of 43 K-pop songs (1,740 lines, 3-8 singers per song) built from crowd annotations verified by independent annotators, together with alignment and scoring tools, and we derive line labels for the IdolSongsJp corpus from its per-singer solo renditions for evaluation on unseen singers. Combining lead-vocal isolation with a karaoke separator, singing-adapted speaker embeddings, and two training-free song-level decoders (a sticky Viterbi pass over line order and unsupervised linking of a group's songs) improves B-cubed F1 over the standard pipeline (vocal separation, speaker embeddings, per-song clustering) by +0.058 on ColorCoded-SD (p=0.001) and by +0.066 on IdolSongsJp (p=0.003). Isolating the lead is the largest single factor wherever the separator leaves a lead voice (+0.04 to +0.06 on the same lines), and with the singers' dry studio takes two different encoders become indistinguishable; the remaining errors concentrate on short lines that carry too little audio for a voiceprint. We also report negative results (more or cleaner training data, weight editing, a song-context model, and target-singer extraction) that bound where further gains can come from.

title: Learning Temporal Stabilization for Double-Talk-Robust Delay Estimation in Acoustic Echo Cancellation
summary: Acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) depends on accurate time-delay estimation (TDE): the adaptive canceller converges only after the bulk delay between the far-end reference and the microphone is compensated. GCC-PHAT remains the standard TDE front-end and, in our stress tests, wins or ties against a fully learned estimator under interference, low SNR, strong reverberation, loudspeaker nonlinearity, and noisy references. Its principal failure mode is short-window sustained double-talk, where near-end speech creates spurious correlation peaks that classical smoothing and confidence gating cannot reliably suppress. We therefore retain GCC-PHAT as a fixed, non-learnable backbone and learn only a 13.2K-parameter causal 2-D CNN stabilizer over the time--lag correlogram. The stabilizer exploits a simple temporal distinction: true delays form persistent ridges, whereas double-talk artifacts appear as transient spikes. Across synthetic and real AEC-Challenge echo paths, it reduces MAE and gross-outlier rates by approximately $3$--$5\x$ over tuned classical estimators and the WebRTC AEC3 matched filter. A faithful AEC3-style downstream testbed further shows that these delay gains translate into lower echo-leak rates and faster post-jump ERLE recovery in time-varying regimes, closing much of the gap to the oracle-delay ceiling. An optional coarse-to-fine pre-alignment stage extends the same residual stabilizer to stable 100--400\,ms bulk delays without retraining, while keeping the learned component focused on short-window double-talk robustness.

title: TigerTTS: Draft-Guided Multi-Frame Parallel Speech-Token Language Model for Fast and Robust Text-to-Speech
summary: Autoregressive speech-token language models enable high-quality TTS but suffer from latency growth with sequence length, word omission or repetition without explicit alignment, and fidelity limits from discrete codebooks. We present TigerTTS, a production-grade LLM TTS system built around a lightweight non-autoregressive NAR model. With explicit alignment, the NAR model drafts tokens for the entire utterance, which are refined frame-by-frame by a compact autoregressive LLM. The draft is aligned frame-for-frame with LLM targets and injected at the input, ensuring training-inference consistency. Leveraging its accuracy, the LLM predicts 12 tokens per step across 3 frames and 4 groups, while a conditional-total-correlation bound keeps parallel prediction nearly lossless. We use a codebook-free FSQ tokenizer with four parallel groups and about 1800 bps to avoid codebook collapse. The backbone keeps positional information only in input embeddings, enabling exact MLA weight absorption and a four-fold KV-cache reduction. Decoding uses CUDA Graphs with a graph-safe multinomial sampler. A Fast mode further reduces first-packet latency: the NAR generator acts as a prefix synthesizer with RTF 0.03, producing the first 500 ms before LLM decoding. With CUDA-Graph decoding, TigerTTS reaches RTF 0.05, about 20x real-time, on one GPU. Despite using a 0.15B backbone, it outperforms standard PyTorch inference of VoxCPM2 2B by 5x and CosyVoice 2 by 16x. TigerTTS achieves the lowest CER and WER on SEED, 1.09 and 1.67, and strong WER, NMOS, and speaker similarity on LibriSpeech test-clean, 2.22, 4.36, and 0.820. Fast-mode guided semantic tokens provide a well-aligned content prior, reducing dropped words, loops, and runaway generation without sacrificing speed.

title: A Head-Level Investigative Study of Self-Supervised Backbones for Synthetic Speech Detection
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech backbones are the standard frontend for synthetic-speech detection, and layer-wise probing has established which layers carry the most signal. But analysis stops there: which of a layer's twelve attention heads compute the spoof decision is unknown. We present the first head-level study of two frozen backbones, WavLM-base and Wav2Vec2-base, on ASVspoof 5. Per-head ablation shows that only a few heads carry the decision while others actively oppose it; removing those heads lowers equal error rate (EER) with no retraining, by 13% relative in WavLM and 22% in Wav2Vec2. We also find a probe-free signature: spoofed speech draws more focused attention than genuine speech, and this gap alone separates the two almost as well as the full representation, peaking at each backbone's most discriminative layer. Finally, attack identity is decodable from every head, yet heads differ in what they do, not in what they know.

title: An offset--drift Kalman filter for continuous emotion recognition and annotation from sparse human reviews
comment: The manuscript is 6 pages long and includes 1 figure and 2 tables. It is planned for submission to INTERSPEECH 2027
summary: Continuous emotion recognition tracks how emotion changes over time, but its predictions often deviate from human ratings, and the traces it is trained on are rated in real time by several annotators, which is slow and costly. A few human reviews could help with both, but rejection only decides which predictions to hand over and adaptation adjusts the model or its outputs; neither uses reviews to correct unreviewed windows directly. We propose a Kalman-filter correction that models the predictor's error as a per-part offset plus a slow drift, estimates it from the reviewed windows and corrects every unreviewed window online, leaving the predictor unchanged. On MSP-Conversation, it beats four simpler corrections in all 48 paired comparisons, keeps correcting each part after reviewing stops and, for uncorrected predictions, tells a person which windows to take over. The same correction serves annotation: with 20% of windows reviewed, the completed trace comes closer to the raters.
